chapterNote: Chapter 23 belongs to the 'Sayings of the Wise' (22:17-24:22) and strings together a series of vivid warnings against misdirected appetite. It opens at the table of a powerful man, where the danger is not the food but the false hospitality (vv. 1-3); it then turns to the feverish chase for wealth that sprouts wings and flies (vv. 4-5), the grudging host whose welcome is a lie (vv. 6-8), and the wasted breath of instructing a fool (v. 9). Against the greedy stand the defenseless — the fatherless, whose Redeemer is mighty (vv. 10-11). The father's voice then pleads tenderly for the son's heart (vv. 12-28), naming the two great appetites that swallow a young man: drink and the strange woman. The chapter climaxes in the unforgettable portrait of the drunkard (vv. 29-35) — the wine that glows red and goes down smooth, but bites at the last like a serpent.

1.text: When you sit down to dine with a ruler, weigh carefully what is set before you,
1.amp: When you sit down [yashab — take your seat, settle in] to eat with a ruler [mashal — one ruling, holding dominion], discern with care [biyn — understand, perceive] what is before [panim — the face, the presence] you;
1.notes: biyn (H995) is repeated for emphasis in the Hebrew — 'discerning, discern' — the alert reading of a situation; mashal (H4910) is to rule, to hold dominion — here, the one governing. The seat of honor at a powerful man's table is a place to keep your wits, not to lose them.

2.text: and put a knife to your own throat if you are a man ruled by his appetite.
2.amp: and set [sum — put, place] a knife [sakkin] to your throat [loa — gullet], if you are a man given [baal — an owner, one mastered by] to appetite [nephesh — the craving soul, the hungering self].
2.notes: the vivid hyperbole means: restrain yourself violently. baal (H1167) is 'owner/master' — but here the man is owned BY his nephesh (H5315), the appetite that should serve him now rules him. Better a blade at the throat than to be enslaved by your own hunger at a ruler's table.

3.text: Do not crave his delicacies, for they are food that deceives.
3.amp: Do not crave [avah — long for, desire keenly] his dainties [matammot — choice, tasty morsels], for they are deceptive [kazab — lying, false] food [lechem — bread].
3.notes: kazab (H3577) is falsehood, a lie — the rich man's feast looks like generosity but conceals a hook; cf. v.6-8 where the same table proves to be no gift at all. matammot (H4303) are the choice, savory morsels; avah (H183) is the deep craving of the appetite the previous verse warned against.

4.text: Do not wear yourself out to get rich; have the wisdom to let it go.
4.amp: Do not weary [yaga — toil, exhaust] yourself to grow rich [ashar — become wealthy]; from your own cleverness [binah — understanding], hold back [chadal — cease, desist, restrain].
4.notes: yaga (H3021) is to labor until spent; chadal (H2308) is to cease and let go. The instruction is not against work but against the frantic, self-driven scramble for wealth — true binah (H998) knows when to stop straining (cf. 1 Tim 6:9-10).

5.text: Will you let your eyes fly after riches that are gone? For wealth surely sprouts wings of its own and flies off to the heavens like an eagle.
5.amp: Will you set your eyes [ayin] flying [uph — fly, soar] after what is not? For riches certainly make [asah] themselves wings [kanaph — wing, edge], and fly away [uph] like an eagle [nesher] toward the heavens [shamayim].
5.notes: uph (H5774), 'to fly,' is doubled in the Hebrew with bitter wit — the eyes 'fly' after wealth, and the wealth 'flies' away faster; the marginal note reads 'cause your eyes to fly upon.' nesher (H5404) is the eagle, the swiftest of birds: riches are here one moment, a vanishing speck the next.

6.text: Do not eat the bread of a stingy man, and do not crave his delicacies;
6.amp: Do not eat the bread [lechem] of one who has an evil [ra — bad, grudging] eye [ayin], and do not crave [avah] his dainties [matammot];
6.notes: the 'evil eye' (ra ayin, H7451 + H5869) is the Hebrew idiom for stinginess and grudging envy, the opposite of the 'good eye' that gives generously (22:9). His matammot (H4303), his dainties, are set out, but his heart begrudges every bite — cf. the counterfeit hospitality unmasked in the next verse.

7.text: for as he calculates the cost within himself, so he truly is. 'Eat and drink!' he says to you, but his heart is not with you.
7.amp: for as he reckons [shaar — thinks, estimates, calculates] within his soul [nephesh], so is he. 'Eat and drink [akal... shatah],' he says [amar] to you, but his heart [leb] is not with you.
7.notes: shaar (H8176) means to reckon up or estimate — he is mentally tallying the cost of every morsel even as he urges you to eat. His words (amar, H559) say welcome; his leb (H3820) says go. The verse exposes the gap between the mouth and the heart.

8.text: The morsel you have eaten you will vomit up, and your kind words will have been wasted on him.
8.amp: The morsel [path] you have eaten [akal] you will vomit up [qo], and you will have wasted [shachat — spoil, ruin] your pleasant [naim] words [dabar].
8.notes: path (H6595) is the morsel and qo (H6958) the vomiting of it up; shachat (H7843) is to spoil or ruin — the courteous flattery you spent to win his favor turns sour and is thrown away with the food. naim (H5273), 'pleasant,' marks the warmth you offered; the whole exchange leaves only nausea and regret.

9.text: Waste no words on the ears of a fool, for the sound sense you offer is the very thing he will hold in contempt.
9.amp: Do not speak [dabar] in the ears [ozen] of a fool [kesil — the thick-headed, willfully dull], for he will despise [buz — hold in contempt] the insight [sekel — prudence, good sense] of your words.
9.notes: kesil (H3684) is the dull fool who will not learn; buz (H936) is contempt. Wisdom poured into such ears is wasted breath — he scorns the very sekel (H7922), the sound sense, you offer (cf. 9:8; Matt 7:6).

10.text: Do not move the ancient boundary stone, and do not push into the fields of the fatherless,
10.amp: Do not remove [nasag — shift back, displace] the ancient [olam — of old, age-long] boundary [gebul — border, landmark], and do not enter [bo] the fields [sadeh] of the fatherless [yatom — the orphan];
10.notes: nasag (H5253) is to displace, to push back; olam (H5769) marks the boundary as age-old, set by the fathers and protected by covenant law (Deut 19:14; 27:17). To move it against the yatom (H3490), the defenseless orphan, is the cruelest theft — robbing the one with no one to defend him; yet see the next verse.

11.text: for their Redeemer is strong; He Himself will take up their case against you.
11.amp: for their Redeemer [goel — the kinsman who buys back, avenges, defends] is mighty [chazaq — strong, fierce]; He will plead [rib — contend, bring suit] their cause [riyb — their legal dispute] against you.
11.notes: goel (H1350) is the kinsman-redeemer, the relative bound to rescue and avenge his helpless kin — here it is God Himself who takes that role for the orphan. He is chazaq (H2389), strong enough to win, and He will rib (H7378) — plead — their riyb (H7379), their lawsuit, against the oppressor in the highest court (cf. Exod 22:22-24; Ps 68:5).

12.text: Bring your heart in under correction, and bend your ears toward whatever words carry knowledge.
12.amp: Bring [bo — bring in, apply] your heart [leb] to discipline [musar — corrective instruction] and your ears [ozen] to the words [emer] of knowledge [daat].
12.notes: musar (H4148) is formative correction, often costly; daat (H1847) is knowledge. The verse turns from warnings to the inward posture wisdom requires — the heart (leb, H3820) applied and the ear bent, the same wholehearted reception commended throughout the book (cf. 2:1-2).

13.text: Do not withhold correction from a child; if you discipline him with the rod, he will not die.
13.amp: Do not withhold [mana — hold back, restrain] correction [musar] from the child [naar — boy, youth]; though you strike [nakah — smite] him with the rod [shebet — staff, rod of discipline], he will not die [muth].
13.notes: shebet (H7626) is the shepherd's staff and the rod of discipline; musar (H4148) is loving correction, not abuse. The point is reassurance to the parent who hesitates: under measured discipline the child will not muth (H4191), die — withholding it is what destroys (cf. 13:24; 22:15).

14.text: You strike him with the rod, and you rescue his soul from the grave.
14.amp: You strike [nakah] him with the rod [shebet], and you deliver [natsal — snatch away, rescue] his soul [nephesh] from Sheol [sheol — the grave, the realm of the dead].
14.notes: natsal (H5337) is to snatch from danger; sheol (H7585) is the realm of the dead. The eternal stakes are named: faithful, loving correction is not cruelty but rescue — it pulls the child back from the path that ends in death (cf. v.13).

15.text: My son, if your heart is wise, then my own heart will be glad — yes, mine.
15.amp: My son [ben], if your heart [leb] is wise [chakam — act wisely], my heart [leb] will rejoice [samach — be glad], even mine [ani — I myself].
15.notes: the father's tenderness breaks through: the son's wise heart (leb, H3820) is its own reward to the parent. The emphatic ani (H589), 'even I,' shows a joy that is personal and intimate — 'mine, of all hearts' — echoed in the parallel of v.16 (cf. 10:1).

16.text: My inmost being will thrill with joy when your lips speak what is upright.
16.amp: My kidneys [kilyah — the innermost self, the seat of deep emotion] will exult [alaz — rejoice triumphantly], when your lips [saphah] speak [dabar] what is right [meyshar — uprightness, straight things].
16.notes: the Hebrews located the deepest feelings in the kilyah (H3629), the kidneys/inward parts; alaz (H5937) is exultant, triumphant joy. The father is moved to the core not by his son's success but by his upright speech, the outflow of a wise heart (cf. v.15).

17.text: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but live in the fear of the LORD all day long.
17.amp: Do not let your heart [leb] envy [qana — be jealous of] sinners [chatta — offenders], but be in the fear [yirah — reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH] all the day [yom] long.
17.notes: qana (H7065) is burning envy — the temptation of the heart (leb, H3820) to covet the prosperity of the wicked (cf. Ps 73). The antidote is not mere restraint but a rival passion: continual yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068), the fear of the LORD, which keeps the heart fixed on a better hope (next verse).

18.text: An outcome is waiting for you, beyond all doubt — and the thread of what you long for will never be severed.
18.amp: For surely there is [yesh — there exists] a future [acharit — a latter end, an outcome]; and your hope [tikvah — expectation, the cord let down] will not be cut off [karat — severed].
18.notes: acharit (H319) is the 'latter end,' the final outcome that vindicates the righteous; tikvah (H8615) comes from a root meaning 'cord' — the lifeline of expectation. Unlike the envied sinner, the God-fearer has a thread that will not be karat (H3772), cut, but holds to the end (cf. 24:14, 20; Jer 29:11).

19.text: Hear, my son, and be wise, and keep your heart on the straight road.
19.amp: Hear [shama — listen and obey], my son [ben], and be wise [chakam], and set straight [ashar — direct, lead on the level path] your heart [leb] in the way [derek].
19.notes: shama (H8085) is hearing that obeys; ashar (H833) here means to guide straight, to lead along a level road. The plea is for the heart (leb, H3820) itself to be steered onto the derek (H1870), the way — not merely outward conduct but the inner direction that governs the feet (cf. 4:23).

20.text: Do not keep company with those who drink themselves drunk, or with those who gorge on meat,
20.amp: Do not be among those who drink too much wine [yayin], among the gluttons [zalal — those who squander, gorge wastefully] of flesh [basar — meat];
20.notes: the warning pairs two appetites left unchecked — drink and food. zalal (H2151) means to be loose, to squander; basar (H1320) is flesh/meat. The company a man keeps shapes his appetites, and these companions feed the very cravings vv. 1-3 warned against (cf. Deut 21:20).

21.text: for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and drowsiness will dress a man in rags.
21.amp: for the drunkard [saba] and the glutton [zalal] will fall into poverty [yarash — be dispossessed], and drowsiness [numah — sleepy stupor] will clothe [labash — dress, put on] a man in rags [qera — tattered scraps].
21.notes: saba (H5433) is the hard drinker, zalal (H2151) the glutton, yarash (H3423) to be dispossessed — the dissolute life follows a predictable arc: indulgence breeds the stupor (numah, H5124) of laziness, laziness breeds want, and want clothes the man in qera (H7168), torn rags. labash (H3847), 'to clothe,' makes poverty itself the garment self-chosen appetite hands out (cf. 6:9-11).

22.text: Give ear to the father who brought you into the world, and when your mother has grown old, never treat her with scorn.
22.amp: Listen [shama] to your father [ab] who begat [yalad — bore, brought you forth] you, and do not despise [buz — hold in contempt] your mother [em] when she is old [zaqen — aged, grown elderly].
22.notes: yalad (H3205) is to give birth/beget — the father who 'gave you life' has a claim no passing years cancel; buz (H936), the same contempt the fool shows wisdom (v.9), must never be turned on an aging mother. Honor for parents is wisdom's near-instinct (cf. Exod 20:12; Prov 30:17).

23.text: Buy the truth and never sell it — wisdom and discipline and understanding too.
23.amp: Buy [qanah — acquire, get for yourself] the truth [emeth — truth, faithfulness], and do not sell [makar] it; also wisdom [chokmah], and discipline [musar], and understanding [binah].
23.notes: qanah (H7069) is to acquire at cost; emeth (H571) is truth that is firm and faithful, the very reliability of God's word. Truth is worth any price to gain and no price to surrender — 'buy, and never sell (makar, H4376)' — and the same is true of the prologue's three treasures, chokmah (H2451), musar (H4148), binah (H998).

24.text: The father of a righteous child will greatly rejoice, and whoever fathers a wise son delights in him.
24.amp: The father [ab] of the righteous [tsaddiq] will greatly [gil] rejoice [gil — exult, spin with joy]; and he who begets [yalad] a wise [chakam] child will be glad [samach] in him.
24.notes: the Hebrew doubles the joy-root gil (H1523/H1524) for intensity — 'rejoicing he will rejoice.' The reward for raising a wise, righteous child is the parent's deep gladness (samach, H8055); this is the harvest the father's pleas (vv. 15-16, 19, 22) are sown toward (cf. 10:1; 15:20).

25.text: Let your father and mother be glad, and let her who bore you rejoice.
25.amp: Let your father [ab] and your mother [em] be glad [samach — rejoice]; and let her who bore [yalad] you exult [gil].
25.notes: the appeal turns direct: live so that your parents' joy (samach, H8055; gil, H1523) is fulfilled. 'Her who bore you' tenderly recalls the mother's travail in giving life — a wise life is the son's truest gift back to those who gave him his (cf. v.22, 24).

26.text: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep watch on my ways.
26.amp: My son [ben], give [natan — grant, hand over] me your heart [leb], and let your eyes [ayin] watch over [natsar — guard, keep] my ways [derek].
26.notes: the father asks for the whole inner man — the leb (H3820), the seat of will and love — not mere outward compliance; natsar (H5341) is to keep close watch. To 'give the heart' and fix the eye on the right path is the hinge before the chapter's gravest warnings (vv. 27-35; cf. 4:23).

27.text: For a prostitute is a deep pit, and the wayward woman a narrow well.
27.amp: For a prostitute [zanah — the harlot, she who goes astray] is a deep [amoq] ditch [shuchah — a pit, a trap]; and the foreign woman [nokriyyah — the strange, off-limits woman] is a narrow [tsar — tight, constricting] well [beer — a pit-shaft].
27.notes: two images of inescapable capture: the deep (amoq, H6013) pit (shuchah, H7745) you fall into and cannot climb out of, and the narrow shaft (beer, H875) that traps you in tighter the deeper you go. zanah (H2181) and nokriyyah — the feminine form of nokriy (H5237) — name the seductress whose path runs down to death (cf. 22:14; 5:3-5).

28.text: She lies in ambush like a robber and multiplies the faithless among men.
28.amp: She also lies in wait [arav — ambushes] like a robber for prey [chetheph], and multiplies [yasaph — adds, increases] the treacherous [bagad — the faithless betrayers] among men [adam].
28.notes: arav (H693), to ambush, casts her as a predator hunting victims; the margin reads 'as a robber.' Her work is not merely personal ruin but social corruption — she yasaph (H3254), increases, the number of the bagad (H898), those who betray faith and break covenant (cf. v.27; 2:17).

29.text: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has quarrels? Who has complaints? Who has wounds for nothing? Who has bloodshot eyes?
29.amp: Who has woe [oy]? Who has sorrow [aboi — alas, grief]? Who has contentions [madon — strife, quarrels]? Who has complaint [siach — muttering, anxious babbling]? Who has wounds [petsa — bruises] without cause [chinnam — for nothing]? Who has redness [chaklilut] of eyes [ayin]?
29.notes: a riddling string of six questions whose answer (v.30) is the drunkard. oy (H188) and aboi (H17) are cries of grief; the needless bruises (petsa, H6482; chinnam, H2600) and bloodshot eyes are the marks drink leaves on body and life alike — self-inflicted misery no one else imposed.

30.text: Those who linger long over wine, who go searching out the blended drink.
30.amp: Those who tarry long [achar — delay, linger] over the wine [yayin]; those who go [bo] to seek out [chaqar — search, explore] mixed wine [mimsak — spiced, blended drink].
30.notes: chaqar (H2713) is to search out and examine — the connoisseur's pursuit, here bent to ruin. The answer to all six questions of v.29 is the man who lingers (achar, H309) at the cup and hunts down the strongest blend (mimsak, H4469); the misery is no mystery, it is the drink itself.

31.text: Do not gaze at the wine when it glows red, when it sparkles in the cup and slips down so smoothly.
31.amp: Do not look [raah — gaze, fix the eyes] at the wine [yayin] when it is red [adam — ruddy, glowing], when it gives its sparkle [ayin — its 'eye,' its gleam] in the cup [kos], when it goes down [halak — moves, glides] smoothly [meyshar — straight, evenly].
31.notes: the seduction is sensory and step by step — color, sparkle, smoothness. Hebrew puns: the wine gives its ayin (H5869, literally 'eye') in the cup, its glittering gleam. raah (H7200), the gazing look, is where the fall begins, just as with the strange woman — the warning is to refuse the first long look (cf. v.33; Gen 3:6).

32.text: In the end it bites like a serpent and strikes its venom like a viper.
32.amp: At the last [acharit — the latter end, the outcome] it bites [nashak — sinks its fangs] like a serpent [nachash], and stings [parash — poisons, spits venom] like an adder [tsiphoni — viper].
32.notes: acharit (H319), the 'latter end' that crowned the righteous man's hope in v.18, here delivers the drunkard his sting; nashak (H5391) is the fang's bite. What glides down sweet and smooth (v.31) ends in the strike of a nachash (H5175) — the serpent's ancient bite, sweet at the lip and deadly at the last.

33.text: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will speak what is twisted.
33.amp: Your eyes [ayin] will see [raah] strange women [zur — strange things, alien sights], and your heart [leb] will utter [dabar — speak] perverse things [tahpukah — twisted, upside-down speech].
33.notes: drink distorts both sight and speech: the eyes raah (H7200) what is strange and unreal (zur, H2114), and the leb (H3820) pours out tahpukah (H8419), the upside-down talk that elsewhere marks the wicked (2:12). Wine unhinges perception from truth and the tongue from sense.

34.text: You will be like one lying down in the heart of the sea, or one sprawled at the top of a swaying mast.
34.amp: Yes, you will be like one who lies down [shakab] in the midst [leb — the 'heart'] of the sea [yam], or like one who lies [shakab] at the top [rosh — head] of the rigging [chibbel — mast, ship's tackle].
34.notes: two pictures of helpless disorientation — the man rolling in the heart (leb, H3820, lit. 'heart of the sea,' per the margin) of the heaving waves, or clinging atop a pitching mast (rosh, H7218). The drunkard has lost all steadiness; the very ground beneath him seems to swing and reel.

35.text: 'They struck me,' you will say, 'but I felt no pain; they beat me, and I never knew it. When will I wake — I will go looking for another drink.'
35.amp: 'They struck [nakah — smote] me,' you will say, 'but I was not hurt [chalah — made sick, wounded]; they beat [halam — hammered] me, and I did not know [yada — felt, was aware of] it. When shall I awake [qits]? I will seek [baqash — search out] it yet again [yasaph — once more].'
35.notes: the chapter ends in the drunkard's own numb voice: blows land (nakah, H5221) and he feels nothing (yada, H3045, 'I knew it not,' per the margin), the surest sign of bondage. Even half-conscious he is already planning the next round — baqash (H1245) again, yasaph (H3254), 'once more' — the perfect, chilling portrait of addiction's grip.
